speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the crisis in the maritime coal industry which has occasioned mass lay-offs because of a steadily declining market for the product of this basic industry of Nova Scotia.

subsubtopic: MASS LAY-OFFS    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: This suggested matter of urgency of debate is one we have heard from time to time in the course of this session. Questions have been asked and pressure has been applied during question time in order to have this matter considered. I should be glad to have advice from those who are familiar with the practice in these matters as to the urgency of debating this subject at this time.

If I may say a word on this point I would draw Your Honour's attention to the fact that it was the impression of my hon. friend from Gloucester and many of us on this side of the house that there would be an opportunity to discuss this matter on the supplementary estimates, and it was for that reason that we refrained at an earlier date from bringing this subject forward in this way. However, as Your Honour may be aware, last evening when the hon. member for Gloucester sought to discuss some of the more pressing aspects of this matter on the item in the supplementary estimates respecting the dominion coal board the chairman ruled him out of order on an interpretation of the item which I, of course, will not discuss because I do not think it would be proper for me to discuss a decision of the Chair.

Before my hon. friend made the proposal he just made for leave to present his motion today, we considered very carefully whether
Nova Scotia-Mass Coal Lay-offs there was any other way a debate could be brought on at an early date. As Your Honour is aware, of course, there has been a considerable lay-off in what is the main industry of the province of Nova Scotia, and there have been repeated attempts from this side of the house to put forward arguments to urge the government to announce its policy without further delay.
It is in order to have an early debate on this subject, and because there seemed to be no other opportunity available in the near future, that my hon. friend has brought this matter forward today.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):

subsubtopic: MASS LAY-OFFS    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Minister of Finance has advanced a very

strange theory in opposition to the motion that the house adjourn to discuss this matter. The argument he put is that because this question is at present under discussion between this government and the provincial government-that of itself is a recognition of the urgency of the matter-we should not be permitted to discuss this matter in the house. I think that is an argument that certainly cannot be allowed to go unchallenged.
The criteria that have been laid down, Mr. Speaker, which should be satisfied before a matter of this kind can be considered as suitable for the adjournment of the house, have been clearly stated in Erskine May, fourteenth edition, page 344. First the matter must be definite. This certainly is definite. Then the matter must be urgent. We submit that this matter is urgent. Indeed, this matter was considered in the provincial house yesterday, and was considered so urgent as to persuade the premier of that province to invite a Nova Scotia coal miner to the floor of the legislature to address the house.
Then, Mr. Speaker, the minister advanced the argument that there has been an opportunity to discuss this matter on the throne speech debate. It should be pointed out that since that debate concluded there has been a deterioration in the coal mining situation in Nova Scotia, to the point where 4,000 miners have been laid off. Therefore as a result of that change in the situation, irrespective of the fact that it might have been discussed in an earlier debate, we submit that this question of urgency is a very real one. The third criterion is that the matter must be of public importance. Surely there can be no argument on that score. Finally, the matter must involve more than ordinary administration of the law.
I submit with great respect, Mr. Speaker, that these four criteria are met by this situation which has been brought to our attention by the hon. member for Gloucester and that therefore you would be justified in accepting this motion and giving us an opportunity to debate at this time, in a constructive helpful way, this very urgent and important situation.

No one, of course, denies for a moment that the problem sought to be discussed here is one of great concern and having very great effect upon those who are suffering from it. However, it is my understanding,
Nova Scotia-Mass Coal Lay-offs and indeed the reference in Beauchesne establishes it, that the problem to be discussed on an occasion such as this must be one of a national nature.
I refer you to subparagraph 5 of citation 100, at page 90 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which points out that the adjournment of the house cannot be moved with reference to critical conditions generally prevailing in certain parts of the country. In making this argument I do not suggest for a moment the situation may not be critical; but it is a situation, so far as the coal mines are concerned, of local application and is therefore not one of those matters of sufficient importance under this rule to warrant the national House of Commons interrupting its debates on matters of national concern.
I refer also to the point which was made the last time a similar motion was sought to be advanced. This relates to whether the matter is under the administrative responsibility of the government. I refer to subparagraph 1 of citation 100, found at page 89 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. It says that the definite matter of urgent public importance for the discussion of which a member may ask leave to move the adjournment of the house must involve the administrative responsibility of the government. It is true that we have items in the estimates and provision is made, I believe under a statute, for subventions with regard to coal and the movement of coal, but I think it is a far cry from that to suggest that the operation of coal mines themselves is within the administrative responsibility of the government.
The purpose of the rule, it seems clear, is to enable the house to consider a matter of urgent significance about which the government can do something and on which it is the responsibility of the government under some accepted heading of responsibility, to take action. I submit that this particular subject does not fall within that category.
Then with respect to the matter of urgency, I may say that the urgency of the subject must be measured in terms of the urgency of other matters to be discussed. After all if the house is trying to assess the urgency of postponing the business that has been set down for that day, then the house is surely entitled to see how urgent is the matter sought to be raised as compared with the matters the house would otherwise be discussing. The fact remains that the miners of Nova Scotia have placed this matter before the federal government, and that the federal government now has a committee set up which is studying it. I do

not see that any good purpose would be served by the matter being discussed further at this time.

subsubtopic: MASS LAY-OFFS    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word on the first point raised by the Minister of Justice, namely that this is a critical matter of a local nature only. The citation referred to by the Minister of Justice, if my memory serves me correctly, refers to a precedent in the year 1818 in the United Kingdom, a rather long time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MASS LAY-OFFS    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: No, no. If my hon. friend will look at it-

subsubtopic: MASS LAY-OFFS    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I wish to direct Your
Honour's attention to a precedent in the year 1957, when Your Honour was considering a similar motion moved by the hon. member for Essex East with relation to the closing down of two motor car factories and the possible closing down of a third motor car factory, all of them situated in the province of Ontario. This will, of course, be in Your Honour's memory; it occurred on December 2, 1957. I would imagine that, important as the motor car industry is to Ontario, the coal mining industry is equally important to Nova Scotia and that if one is national, as I maintain it is, the other is also national. For that reason, if the precedent set by Your Honour was a good one, as I believe it was, then the hon. member for Gloucester is on sound ground in following that precedent.
On the second point, that this matter does not come within the administrative jurisdiction of parliament, may I say that the hon. member for Gloucester is not suggesting the nationalization of the mines or anything having to do with property and civil rights. He is suggesting something that has historically been under the control of parliament, a matter that a special agency has been set up to deal with, namely the dominion coal board; a matter which has been dealt with by royal commissions appointed by federal governments and a matter, incidentally, for which members of the present government claimed to have a solution before they came into office. So it does seem to me that this argument falls to the ground.
On the question of previous opportunities, I think I indicated to Your Honour that it was our belief that we would have an opportunity when the supplementary estimates came up, and that we had deferred this matter until that time but then found that we did not have that opportunity. Of course it is within Your Honour's memory that the lay-offs took place subsequent to the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. We also have not been told when the government next proposes to move a motion to go into supply.
Nova Scotia-Mass Coal Lay-offs
So there is no early prospect of a debate, except one, sir. I venture to suggest to the government that if they do not want to have the proceedings today interrupted there is one way in which that can be avoided. I am making this suggestion directly to the Prime Minister, if I may. I suggest that the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys be withdrawn from the standing committee on mines, forests and waters, brought back to the house and called on Friday next. If the government is prepared to do that, then I am sure the hon. member for Gloucester would be quite happy not to proceed with this motion. Otherwise, sir, there does not seem to be any early opportunity to discuss this national matter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MASS LAY-OFFS    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not going to put forward an argument with regard to the technical question, but I do want to answer the last suggestion of the hon. gentleman. Only two days ago, as you will recall, sir, I was condemned because I had said that if any unfairness took place I would see that it was rectified. My hon. friend now asks me to change an order of the house whereby this particular matter was sent to a committee, and to alter that order. That argument does not come very well from him.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MASS LAY-OFFS    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
In dealing with this matter may I say at the outset that I do not accept the proposition that because it affects only the Nova Scotia coal industry it is therefore not a fit subject for a motion of this kind. Hon. members can set their minds at rest on that point. Before giving my view, may I recall that what we are asked to debate today is the crisis in the maritime coal industry which has occasioned mass lay-offs because of a steadily declining market for the basic industry of Nova Scotia. The subject really is the crisis in the maritime coal industry because of a steadily declining market.
There is no doubt that this is a very important matter, and I do not think anyone in the house has attempted to say anything different. It is an important matter, and it is particularly important to the people who are immediately affected. It perhaps is a part of the general important problem of unemployment. The difficulty I have had with this request is that it perhaps is a localized or specific aspect of the unemployment problem. If the subject were just unemployment generally I would refuse the motion without hesitation.
The question in my mind has been whether the situation here is of such a nature that it is different from the continuing problem. It has been suggested that because of certain

Motions for Papers
recent lay-ofis there is something urgent, immediate and imminent about this matter which makes it different today from what it has been thus far during the session. I am not prepared to accept that view. I think what has happened recently, which has perhaps impelled the hon. member to attempt to bring this matter before the house, is the recent lay-offs; but as he phrased his motion it refers to the continually declining market and as such that is a matter which has been capable of discusion right from the first of the session. In fact it was discussed, as has been pointed out, in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, has been raised certainly half a dozen times to my knowledge on the orders of the day, and was discussed, I believe, in a limited way yesterday.
Therefore, though I do have some reservations about the soundness of my view, I am not prepared at the moment to decide that we should interrupt our proceedings to discuss this matter at this precise time.

This question arises from certain publicity given this matter which appeared in Winnipeg newspapers.
I have here an article from the Winnipeg Free Press dated January 12, 1959, which bears a rather substantial and prominent headline reading, "I Hand Out the Jobs Says Minnedosa Tory." An article which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune on January 14, bears this headline, "Three M.P.s Pick Needy for Park Project Jobs." There is also another article which appeared in the Free Press.

As we all know, the gentleman to whom I have reference is the former minister of justice, Mr. Garson. I believe the committee would be interested in hearing the views of this former member. The following is an extract from an article which appeared in the Tribune of February 6:
Former federal cabinet minister Stuart Garson broke the silence of political retirement Thursday to blast Conservative accusations that local Liberal M.P.s conducted an employment agency in Riding Mountain national park.
[Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria).
This accusation is "so silly, so childish and so cheap," said Mr. Garson in a prepared statement.
Resources Minister Alvin Hamilton said in the commons that the government had followed the practice of the Liberal administration in hiring temporary workers through local advisers. Hiring is now done by the national employment service.

He referred to certain action taken by him in consultation with some of his colleagues and he used the phrase "last fall". I have indicated that certain publicity was given to this matter in the middle of January. I should like the minister to inform the committee what advisers were used by the former member for Marquette in this respect. I should also like him to inform us as to whether there was any release on the part of his colleagues, the hon. members for Marquette, Brandon-Souris and Dauphin-as he said, "last fall"-or whether they actually post-dated the publicity with respect to this matter which I indicated appeared about the middle of January.
I believe the minister was extremely broad and definite in the sweeping accusations he made. Because it involves a former hon. member of this house I feel it is quite worthy of the attention of the public accounts committee. I wonder if the minister would indicate if he would approve of having the park superintendent and if necessary the former hon. member for Marquette or any of his advisers called before the committee to give evidence in connection with the statement made in this house on February 4 of this year.
In addition to that I should very much like to know what the minister meant when he indicated that now there is a certain regularization of procedures in collaboration with the employment service. Does this mean that these agents of the present hon. member for Marquette are still functioning in effect and that the employment agency is simply advised of what he has done? Is that what is meant by "collaboration with the employment service?" I wonder if the minister would give us more detail with respect to this matter before we permit the item to pass.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I intended to
pursue this matter too, because it was my question which led to the statement about which the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River spoke. I share some of his views in this matter but I wish to approach it from a different point of view.
The minister will recall that when the question of national parks was under discussion last year he became somewhat rattled under certain pressures from the opposition with regard to the principle involved in

hiring people for jobs of this nature in national parks. I want to ask him if he honestly believes, no matter how highly he may rate the fairness of the hon. members to whom reference has been made-and certainly the hon. member for Brandon in my opinion is as fair as any hon. member in this committee -that it is possible for them to be completely objective in this respect without regard to party affiliation. The fact remains the hon. member for Brandon-Souris is a politician and a Conservative one at that. If he is able to act fairly irrespective of party affiliation I feel he is perhaps more able than any person in this committee. I know from the experience in my riding with regard to provincial matters where this sort of thing goes on you very often see that the people who are slipped into these jobs are required to take out membership in the Conservative party. I am not suggesting that this is the case at all but one is bound to have such suspicions until the whole thing is regularized as the minister suggested was being done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I notice that some hon. members jeer at this but it is an unusual arrangement and I feel we need a more adequate explanation than this. When we have a national employment service I fail to see why it should not be used in this regard. I do not feel that a member of parliament is more competent to select people for jobs than the employment service. That is the function of the employment service and is not a duty of a member of parliament. I was dissatisfied with the statement at the time the minister made it and I would certainly welcome additional information about the procedure. I agree with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River that the imputation made with regard to the reputation of a former member might well be considered in the public accounts committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I was rather surprised at the question asked by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and originally asked during this session by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate regarding the employment on winter works that we now have under discussion. I can understand the confusion of the hon. member for Port Arthur who has to rely on that very fine newspaper, the Free Press, for his information, but, in the case of the two members directly opposite me I thought I had squelched this matter once and for all last session, on a similar vote in the main estimates by saying very bluntly and sincerely that this
Supply-Northern Affairs party had lifted the whole question of employment in the parks to a new high level which I thought the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate wanted. I pointed out that all they could point to among the thousands of employees who were working on this program, or working permanently on the winter works program, were three cases and two more at the last part of the last session and I thought the most effective answer I could give was to repeat at that time what I said at the last session, that even if there were five-and I do not know of five-dismissed since this government took over, all I can say is when you compare that figure with the literally hundreds, indeed the thousands who were dismissed in 1935-and some of us here have personal knowledge of that-and the complete wholesale eliminations, well, this government has lifted employment in the parks to a new high level.
I do not want the committee to take my word for it. I have said in the house that I have asked religious groups and all those who know the needs of the most needy families in the communities-because this is work that has been pushed hard by our department to try to give help where it is most needed

to inform us on the matter. What I would like to do is to settle this once and for all, and I think that is what will happen when I give the source of these letters. These are neutral people, people who are really interested in employing people who need help. This is a letter dated December 27, 1958, and I shall make it available to the house. It is addressed to the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria and reads as follows:
Wreck Cove, Nova Scotia, December 27, 1958.
Mr. Robert Muir, M.P.,
Sydney Mines, Nova Scotia.
Dear Sir:
The work at the shore at Wreck Cove, which has been under way since November 10 is just about completed.
If there had been any discrimination in connection with the employing of men on this project, you would have been advised of same before now, so since there was none I think it only fair to advise you accordingly.
This work under the foremanship of Alex Smith has been carried on in a very fine manner. All the available men in a given area were employed on this project without any consideration as to political affiliations.
We want you to know, as well as Mr. Smith, that we deeply appreciate the fairness shown in employing men at Wreck Cove.
Wishing you the compliments of the season, I am Yours truly,
NORMAN MacASKILL, President,
Victoria County Liberal Association

Supply-Northern Affairs
This is another letter addressed to the same member of parliament and is from the parish priest of St. Joseph's parish. The letter reads:
St. Joseph's Parish, Dingwall, Nova Scotia, January 2, 1959.
Mr. Robert Muir, M.P.,
Cape Breton North and Victoria,
Sydney Mines, Nova Scotia.
Dear Bob:
Just a note to thank you for your successful efforts on behalf of Walter Asaff. He is now at work thanks to you.
I do hope that 1959 will bring you happiness and success.
Sincerely yours,
Frank Morley.
Let us go back to the Riding Mountain national park because the story of the Riding Mountain national park is a perfect example of one type of press that we have to deal with in western Canada. It is not new to us.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The Winnipeg Tribune.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
It is not new
to us to have a group of people as in the city of Brandon deliberately set out to build up a news story, as they did, and to get it published in the newspapers and over the radio in Winnipeg, with the sole purpose of trying to smear a government which has made an effort to increase the standards of employment in the parks. With that information I think the house can take for granted the opinion which we hold of this group of men who deliberately set out to do such a thing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question? Can he tell the committee who composes the group of men he talks about?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris is not in his seat. He knows the story and when the appropriate time comes possibly I will -ask him to tell the house just exactly who were in that party, who they are and what positions they hold in the Liberal party.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister has made a very serious charge against a group of men in Brandon. I am asking whether he will substantiate that charge and name the people he is talking about.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I will deal with the former minister of justice, the former member for Marquette, right now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Put up.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Let me finish my statement. This question was asked me today by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy

River and referred to the statement by the ex-minister of justice, Hon. Mr. Garson, who said that he did not know there was anything going on. I am, of course, paraphrasing what the hon. member read.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I did not say that at all. I asked the minister who were the advisers he mentioned in his statement dated February 4?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: You are going to find out.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Good.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
When I heard of this whole story in the press I knew that negotiations had been going on to set up the best way to carry out employment in those parks and particularly in Riding Mountain national park. This press publicity came to my attention and I immediately inquired as to what was the practice in Riding Mountain national park in the time since we had taken office and prior to that, and the information came from my department that the system in use in Riding Mountain national park in the first year after we came into power was the same as had been used by the previous administration, and this system was well known to everybody in that whole area. I was told that the people in that area of the Riding Mountain national park who wanted employment reported to people who they were told to see, and those people gave a list to the superintendent and this superintendent, as the opportunities became available, employed those people.
My point is this. When I found out that this practice was being followed in my department and this group of men from the ridings around were called in I stated very flatly that the policy of the government on this type of thing was that the national employment service should do the same thing for Riding Mountain national park as it did for the other parks and they agreed that if any person approached them or any of their supporters or organizers or anything of the sort, that these men were to be sent to the national employment service and that was the end of it. I read that statement in the house and I have my statement here.
As for the former minister of justice saying that he did not have anything to do with it, that only indicates to me of how necessary it was to defeat the previous administration. When ministers of the crown did not even know what was going on in their own ridings and left this to an echelon of people more powerful than the member himself to decide who got jobs, then it was about time we cleaned house.

The hon. member for Port Arthur raised the question of Jasper park and I am going to be quite candid. I thought I was speaking on winter works today, but this has no reference to winter works and I do not know whether the chairman will rule me out of order or not. Since he raised it, I should like to suggest I was not rattled. I knew precisely every step that happened last year. If you would go to Jasper park, as I did this last summer and inquire personally into this thing to verify the representations that had been made to me, you would find out what I found. My only regret was that they even went through this courtesy of doing what they did. They should have been dismissed and the reasons stated publicly.
The hon. member for Port Arthur spoke kindly of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. I can join in what he has said because no member of parliament on either side of this house could be more fair than the hon. member for Brandon-Souris has been. All the members around that district have tried to do the best they could in connection with this work. I can give the house the assurance that these letters that you have heard me read here today are verified by the representations of the people who are working on these jobs and who have never even seen a member of parliament. They have obtained their jobs because they were unemployed, and they are very grateful for them. The only complaint I have heard is from a man who hires people in that district. He says it is very hard for him to get people because they all want to work for us in the parks. That is the only complaint I have heard. I was quite honest when I told the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that I had not heard any complaint. I can honestly say that not a single one has come to me. I have tried my best to make this employment program do what it was designed to do.
I should like to come right back to the vote and say one word of explanation on this whole program. It will have become clear to discerning members of the house that the government's winter works program is divided into three parts. The first part concerns works done by the federal government itself through the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Transport and other departments, including my own. Therefore, this item No. 711 is an example of the type of thing that the federal government is doing all by itself. Now, the total of all these things comes to approximately $750 million. Our particular item here looks very small in relation to the whole total, but I shall add some things to it in a moment.
The second part of the program is a cooperative program between the federal
Supply-Northern Affairs government and the provincial government, carried out by my department. This cooperative program is composed of the camp grounds and picnic site program; the forest access roads program and, to a limited degree, the trans-Canada picnic grounds program. These two items that are being used are based on 50 per cent labour, in which all the provinces with one exception are co-operating.
The third part of the program is the municipal works program which is handled by the Minister of Labour, under which we deal through the provinces and the municipalities and where the people who have a local knowledge can recommend the types of work needed in those areas. It is not necessary for the federal government to have a tremendous staff to handle the works programs in these areas. My problem is having to deal with a permanent staff and when we put on a selective winter works program, trying to aim at the people who need it the most, I have to do it with the people who are normally employed. It depends on this selective idea, and I think it can be worked out with the local people.
This vote No. 711 deals with the work in the national parks and historic sites and totals $2.8 million. At this time, I should like to point out that in the main estimates this vote amounted to $14,399,925. Out of the main estimates we were able to provide $300,000 for a winter works program. In addition, last session we put through a supplementary estimate for $500,000 for this item. Therefore when we total up the amount from the main estimate, the supplementary estimate and this further supplementary estimate, we find that for this one project for winter work we have a total vote of approximately $3.6 million.
I should like to give the house the figures on employment, the actual number of people working on this program. If I may, I should like to give the figures for both votes 711 and 712, the program that affects my department, and then it will save me repeating it. I should have mentioned, in connection with the cooperative program, the roads to resources program which is in full swing. This is another type of co-operative work with the provinces.
In so far as the number employed is concerned, these are the figures for the first week in January, which are the latest I have available. The number of men employed on the roads to resources program is 688; the number on camp grounds and picnic program-total 1,122; on the forest access roads program, 1,366; on the construction program in the territories, 1,492; and the number employed in the parks under this vote we are now discussing is 1,700. This makes a grand total of

Supply-Northern Affairs 6,368 in the first week of January. I recognize that this, by comparison with the tremendous number employed in work for other departments may seem small, but I do suggest that it has been a substantial effort to try to meet seasonal unemployment where we could. I could give a further breakdown of these figures, but unless I am asked I will not hold up the committee by giving such a breakdown.
Hon. members may wish to ask me for a breakdown by provinces of the actual figures. I think I will allow the committee to decide whether or not they want that information. There is one thing more, Mr. Chairman; may I go on and make an explanation covering the next vote?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think we should deal with these items one at a time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I have seldom seen a minister so anxious to avoid a very simple and direct question. I asked him if he would indicate who these advisers were to whom he referred in his statement on February 4. I asked him, in addition, whether or not instead of smearing people in Brandon, he would name them. I can only judge that he must be referring to the winter employment committee in Brandon. The winter employment committee of Brandon, so far as I know, is a non-partisan organization. Apparently they felt it was an undesirable thing to have people engaged on the basis of political patronage through the campaign manager of the hon. member for Marquette rather than on the basis of need. Evidently they issued a statement to the effect that the only way they could see to be certain that the money being spent at the park to relieve unemployment was being used effectively was to use the unemployment insurance offices.
I asked the minister another very direct question. I have the utmost respect for the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, who is not in the house to speak for himself, but the minister brought him in on February 4 by referring to him. Now, I ask him very simply, and very definitely, did the hon. member for Brandon-Souris make these representations to the minister acquiescing in a new scheme before or after this publicity in January or the complaint of the Brandon winter employment committee in December?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I can only refer you to my statement made here on February 4 in which I said, as recorded on page 673 of Hansard for that date:
However, this fall, in view of the vigorous winter work campaign, my office contacted the members for Marquette, Brandon-Souris and Dauphin, suggesting that every effort should be made to ensure

that the most needy cases should be given first consideration in the national park area, irrespective of party affiliations.
The hon. member talked about news stories. In glancing through some of them now I see that they are all dated in January, January 12, January 14, and so on. When I say that I met these people in the fall I do not mean January of 1959. I met them in the fall but I would have to go back and examine my records to see when the meeting took place. I do not have the information here.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The article from which I have already quoted went on to say that at the December meeting of the Brandon winter employment committee the hon. member for Brandon-Souris was present and said that he was aware of this situation and of this type of hiring at Riding Mountain national park and promised the committee that he would call a meeting on his return to Ottawa to look into the matter. The minister should recall this particular circumstance. When he gives the committee the impression that this was done, to use his words, last fall, one would think in terms of September or October and that is a great deal different from some action taken by his colleagues in Manitoba after public complaint had been made.
The other question is still unanswered. Is this group in Brandon, which the minister seemingly was smearing, the winter employment committee to which reference has been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have seen the names but I cannot recall them. The information is in the possession of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. He tells me that he is prepared to stand up in the house and, if it is required, bring the whole matter to the attention of the house. I am going to ask him to do that in view of the statements made and questions asked by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister made a very harsh accusation against a body of citizens in Brandon. Surely he should tell us to what body he is referring. In justice to the citizens winter employment committee of Brandon he should tell us whether that is or is not the body about which he was talking.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am almost positive that it is not the body known as the winter employment committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In the details of the item on page 8 there is an amount of $157,000 for historic sites and an amount of $1,113,500 for national parks trunk highways. Can the minister say what portion of these amounts is being or will be spent in the province of Quebec? He has also talked about a co-operative program

between the federal government and the provinces. Will the minister tell the committee what co-operative program exists now between the province of Quebec and the federal government? Will he also tell the committee how many people in Quebec have been employed by virtue of the co-operative program he has mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The answer on this point is very clear. There are no cooperative road agreements with the province of Quebec.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to return to my point and tell the minister that I read more than the Free Press. I will agree with him that perhaps it has a very sleazy bias but I try to counter that by reading the reactionary pages of the Winnipeg Tribune. I want to come back to the statement of the minister that he sent a letter to these three members of parliament asking them to suggest needy cases and saying to them, "Now, don't pay any attention to party affiliation". I understood him to mean that what he is suggesting is a much better way of doing it than was the case under the old regime.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
One of the maritime members says "hear, hear." Those of us who have a certain detachment and who have never had political patronage at our disposal have noticed that there has been an undercurrent of feeling among some government members that there should be more patronage handed out. Those of us who are detached to a certain extent have rather admired the stand, especially of the Minister of Public Works who, we understand, has taken a pretty firm line against this kind of hand-out. I understand he has done so much to the discomfort of some of the government members but we admire him for it.
But here we have the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and I do not doubt his idealism any more than that of the Minister of Public Works, asking members of parliament to suggest people for jobs. Did he do this because the national employment service could not do the job? Does he not think it would be much better in every case where government jobs are involved that the national employment service or the civil service commission should handle the matter and not members of parliament? That is what I want to get at. I want to secure acceptance of that position and perhaps recognition that, as far as the parks are concerned, his department is working towards that end.
One suggestion which I know has been forwarded to his department is that a federal
Supply-Northern Affairs park be established in the Mount McKay region in the vicinity of Fort William. I am sure that problems would descend upon any member of parliament from that area if this policy were extended in this way. I can see people knocking on the doors and it becoming something that could impinge upon and get in the way of duties of the members of parliament. I think there is a principle involved and I should like a clearer statement of the factors set out in the letter that went to these members and also the role of the national employment service. I should like to say that I do not think it is a question of our swallowing holus-bolus any line that may come out of Brandon or appear in the pages of the Winnipeg Free Press.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think the hon. member has asked a fair question and I am sorry that I have not been able to make my position clear. In areas where there are national employment offices close by what I like the department to do when they need men for these jobs is to go to the national employment offices and the superintendent will hire the men. There has been no trouble in the great majority of the parks, but there are certain parks a long way removed from the national employment offices and we do have a policy of employing men who live close to the parks. This applies particularly in the case of Terra Nova park in Newfoundland and the park in Cape Breton. In those districts we have asked people of varying qualifications, ministers of churches, parish priests and so on, to bring to our attention needy people in order to put them to work. We have considered other things such as rotation to make the work go farther and so on. Generally speaking, there has been a pretty fair effort made to move in that direction.
I was quite surprised when I read this material in the Tribune and Free Press because I do know that we had a discussion in the fall-I cannot give the date without checking my notes-at which the question was raised of whether farmers in the vicinity of Riding Mountain park should be included in the national employment service list. I know that I approved the idea of hiring these farmers if they could be recommended. That is about all I can say. To my knowledge there have been no complaints from the western parks. There were some complaints last year, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate knows, with regard to eastern parks, but I think that on the whole the administration has been such as to be relatively free of complaints. I think this has been a big help to members of parliament of all parties in that they have been able to get away from hiring on a strictly party basis. It has taken

Supply-Northern Affairs the pressure off them and it makes my relationship with my parks people that much better. I do not know what else I can add.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since the minister has frequently made reference to me and since he made reference to the answer he gave me on February 4, I want to make one or two observations which I do not think will be very controversial. I did think that the minister was a little less than fair in the statement he made on February 4 in answer to my first question when he said, as found on page 682 of Hansard:
I would like to thank the hon. member for making representations to me to see that certain people he knows got employment there.
I cannot help but feel that the minister was perhaps not being his usual objective self when he made that statement. The minister knows that he had precisely one letter from me about an individual. His name was Charles Pelley, and I have never seen him in my life to my knowledge, as I said in the letter. He was a veteran from the navy who had heard that there were going to be boats used in connection with the park, and was rather interested in finding out if he could get employment. I sent a letter to the minister about that. As I say, to this day, if I have seen Mr. Pelley I did not know I had seen him.
I have on several occasions written to the minister about the undertaking given by the St. Laurent government, and repeated by the minister in this house, that preference in employment would be given in the Terra Nova national park to those persons who, before the park was established, made their living either by cutting timber in the park or working in sawmills which used the timber which was cut in the park. It did come to my attention that there was a considerable number of these people in Happy Adventure, in Canning's Cove, and in Charlottetown, in particular, who had made their living that way and had great difficulty in getting employment in the park.
I know that the minister has not unlimited opportunities for employment in the park, and I do not think the minister can say I have been in the slightest degree unreasonable about it; but I would submit that that undertaking given by both governments should be vigorously carried out. I wrote to the minister and gave him the name of the principal timber operator in each of these three places. I said that if there was any difficulty about finding out which people did in fact make their living in that way in the park, these would be the people who would most likely have the local knowledge.


I agree with what the minister said just now about the unsuitability of using the employment service as far as Terra Nova national park is concerned, because the nearest employment office is either at St. John's or Grand Falls, in both cases a very considerable distance away from the park. If the employment service were used, particularly this winter when, as all hon. members know, there is so much unemployment in Newfoundland, and when so many people who are unemployed no longer have stamps, I think it would be found that the people who need the work most would not be registered in the employment office at all, and would therefore be overlooked. If one went to another agency it would be better to go to the public assistance or welfare officers, because they are the ones who know the cases of greatest need. I suggest that there is an express obligation, in the case of the Terra Nova national park, to carry out this policy of giving a livelihood first to the people whose livelihood was taken away by the establishment of the park. I believe that the minister and his officials have been trying to do that: I do not think it has always been done. Since the minister, in his reply to the hon. member for Port Arthur, did say that in cases like the Terra Nova national park advice was sought from other quarters-I must say I do not expect the minister to seek my advice, and I do not ask him to; I am realistic about these things-I would be very interested to know whose advice the minister does seek.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think the hon. member knows that I answered that question last session. The gentleman I referred to in that answer had explicit instructions to consider the towns close by. Twenty-five persons from the town of Charlottetown, which the hon. member mentioned, have been employed, and we extended the season for cutting timber. But as the hon. member knows, we have had a terrific time trying to keep people in Newfoundland employed this winter. The letter he sent me was sent on, the same as any other letter is; and I understand that one of the men he has never seen, I presume in Cape Breton, is now working, so his representations have the same effect as any others.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The man I referred to whom I had never seen was from Newfoundland. I do not think I have ever written to the minister about Cape Breton. I did raise a question in the house about a letter I had received from somebody whom I had never seen before; but I did not write to the minister about any place except Terra Nova.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I think that clears up the matter. When the hon. member raised last year in the house these names he said he had not seen them and did not know the person who had written. But I did inquire into it, and I see one of those persons has a job now. I am simply pointing out that representations made by the hon. member are getting back down along the line. So far there have been no complaints, and I hope it will continue that way.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):

I have on different occasions contacted different members of the clergy of the two great religious bodies in regard to people who needed employment. In a rural area they usually know who is hungry and who needs work. That is one of the reasons I made the approach. I have also approached others in the area with regard to hiring, no matter who they were, and I have tried to do the best I could. I have evidence of that and can prove it. Mr. Chairman, I have sat very quietly here for the greater part of yesterday and today but I cannot allow this item to go by without saying a word or two with regard to it because I am a member of a group which is interested not in patronage of human beings but in the proper kind of patronage applied to the forest growth of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member speaking on item 712?

I thought my remarks would indicate that I was. I am one who has lived in the forest all my life and I am particularly interested in these matters. We in this group have no hesitation about supporting this item; our only criticism is that it should be very much larger. We shall have more to say when the main estimates come up for discussion later, but, as I indicated, I cannot refrain from saying a few words at this time.
There is a general feeling in the province of British Columbia, not only among those engaged in the forest industry but among the people generally who realize the extent of the forest wealth we have, and the great need to protect it, that the federal government has not accepted to the full its responsibility with respect to providing funds for building access trails and providing fire fighting equipment. This opinion is indicated in an editorial article recently published in the Vancouver Province which, as hon. members know, is a paper which generally supports this government. This editorial states that the present contribution by the federal government under such items as we are now discussing is a disgracefully low contribution toward the protection of British Columbia forests. I am sure the minister agrees

with this statement in principle and I am sure he will welcome any support he can get here in the house as an indication of the very strong feeling which exists on this question not only in British Columbia but in other parts of Canada.
Last year we had an unusually serious forest fire situation. I understand that about $10 million in stumpage value was lost in British Columbia alone, and this is only the minor aspect of the total loss. There is also the loss in uncommercial growth, the loss of flood protection which forests provide and the loss of the beneficial effect which forests have on climate, to say nothing of the destruction of wild life and the loss of natural beauty. In addition, if my information is correct, there was expended a sum approaching $10 million in all by the government of British Columbia and by the industry concerned in fighting fires during the fire season of 1958. This is in addition to the other losses I have already mentioned, and this is the amount which has been spent in a single season.
I do urge the government to realize that it obtains a tremendous revenue from the forest industry of British Columbia. The government has, in fact, an important stake in the forest industry of the province from which I come, because of the taxes which are paid by the corporations and by the employees concerned. Even from a commonsense point of view, in order to protect this investment the government would be well advised to greatly increase the grants made toward forest protection in the provinces. Before concluding I should like to ask the minister if he has received representations in recent months from organizations or persons interested in seeking an increase in these grants.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: With regard to the observations made by the hon. member for Kootenay West, may I say that I do not think there is any Canadian who recognizes the importance of the woods industry to Canada who would not like to see the expenditure on access roads through our forests greater than it is. The prosperity of the province depends upon the success of the industry and this affects the contributions of the province in terms of corporation and income taxes.
As the hon. member for Kootenay West pointed out, British Columbia was hard hit last year owing to an unusually dry season involving a substantial loss in mature timber, the closing of campsites because of forest fires and the expenditure of approximately $10 million in the fighting of fires. Of the federal government?

speechtext: Yes.

I would like to make a few brief remarks and address a few questions to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I think the vote we are

Supply-Northern Affairs discussing at the present time must be foremost in his program. Last year, when debating this item on the estimates, I had occasion to try to obtain certain information from the minister as to what was to appear in his program. Most of the answers were vague and negative and were to the effect that at that time there were no co-operative schemes with Ontario for example, with respect to roads for forest purposes or for other purposes such as reaching resources such as new timber, mines all of which are very prominent in the area which I represent, namely the Nickel Belt riding.
I have stated that the answers I received last year were vague. The program as laid down last year was more or less a type of revision. I feel that on this occasion I may be able to find out just what is going on in the province of Ontario, and especially in northern Ontario and in my area. The minister said that he operates under a cooperative scheme with the provinces. He said a moment ago that in most of these projects he is not entitled to publicize what the arrangement was or what work was going on. I feel that a project so worthy as this should be understood and that everyone, especially those persons whom it may benefit, should have the information. I fail to see the reasoning behind the minister's statement. I realize that if we are to have agreements with the provincial governments we should have something to say about them. I fail to understand the reference that when there is an agreement with the provinces it should be kept quiet and there should be no publicity about it.
As I travel around my area some people tell me about the access roads of the department of northern affairs. Others tell me about the wonderful work the government in Toronto is doing and no one knows just who the Canadians are who have to do with this problem of developing our resources and reaching them.
It has often been said that the one at the oars is never the one to rock the boat. I feel that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources has placed himself at the oars and is trying to do something which is good and the provincial governments are rocking the boat. If that is so we should ascertain that at this time. We should have certain control over the program and the assistance which we are giving and we should at least know about the resources in my area. I understand that some technical work has been going on.
I should like to know at this time whether there is an agreement with Ontario, what it is and what it means, and if it applies to

northern Ontario. We know that in this area of Ontario there is a place where you do not have to fool the people all the time but only during a forthcoming provincial election. Unfortunately, I received this information only this morning and it pertains to this very matter. The minister may have received the same information. There are problems north of Gogama where certain roads are discussed. I do not know myself exactly what scheme he has in mind, but possibly it follows the theory that the minister has, I feel wrongly, undertaken to follow, namely a co-operative scheme without letting the people know about it.
There is an Indian reserve in my area upon which there is a great deal of timber, possibly some mining wealth and tourist attractions as well. This morning I received a report from Mr. R. Labbe of Gogama and I should like the minister to take note of the conditions to which he referred. The letter says:
The reserve is situated 14 miles northeast of Gogama and there is a good road leading to it but it is not kept open in the winter when it would be mostly needed. Why? No logical explanation can be given. Is it through lack of equipment? Certainly not. The department of highways keeps the road coming into Gogama open all winter. Furthermore, the department of lands and forests keeps five miles of the reserve road open for access to the Gogama-Timmins road now under construction. Two weeks ago, it took the hydro snowmobile six hours to reach the reserve in order to take out an old Indian who had frozen his hands. Two days ago a nurse had to be flown in to get a sick baby to the hospital.
If I might make a comment here, it would seem to me that in these agreements with the provinces there should be an obligation on the province to keep the roads open once they are built with the moneys we are voting. We are voting an amount of $1,682,000, and this is only a supplementary amount to that already voted to the minister for this purpose. Certainly the people need these roads if the resources are to be developed. People will live near these roads, and they should be kept open to assist the people in obtaining the services they need in trying to develop these resources.
I should like to inform the minister of two other incidents which occurred just north of Gogama in my riding. I have a report from the same person, Mr. R. Labbe of Gogama, which reads as follows:
A week ago, I noticed that no smoke was coming out of a shack occupied by a pensioner aged 77. After knocking the door open, we found him lying on the floor face down. He had been dead for six or seven hours. He had tried to light his stove but without success. Water was frozen in the kettle indicating that there had been no fire in the shack for at least 24 hours. Only a few frozen potatoes, a piece of salt pork and a few pieces of bread were found. The shack was so dirty and

m such a mess that the constable who investigated could hardly believe his eyes. Last week, another old age pensioner (80 years) living alone in the bush was found on a lake crawling on all fours not knowing how to get back to his camp. His hands, legs and feet were frozen and doctors are at a loss to explain how he survived. This is legal cruelty to humans.
Of course, the last remark is only the opinion of the person writing the letter. In any event, it appears that this hamlet on the reserve only 14 miles from a proper town in my area is without a road for some seven or eight miles during the wintertime, by means of which they could communicate with civilization. I would, therefore, like to obtain from the minister more information as to what is occurring in so far as Ontario is concerned. How much are they rocking the boat while we are trying to pull at the oars? In what fashion can we ascertain that the people who are serviced by these roads will be able to use them during the winter months, especially in northern Ontario where winter extends over five or six months in the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I have to say very bluntly to my hon. friend that he misunderstands the purpose of this program. This vote is for forest access roads and the program is deliberately designed to make forests accessible for management purposes or in case of fire fighting in the summertime. By no stretch of the imagination does it deal with people at all. The scheme does not relate to roads from A to B or community to community. This roads program proposed by the federal government is to help protect our forests and aid in their management; that is the first thing I should like to say.
I think, myself, that the hon. member has enunciated a very controversial proposition. He says that the federal government should interfere with the provincial government in the conduct of affairs which are expressly in the hands of the provincial government. We would not consider it right to tell any province what they have to do in so far as matters under provincial jurisdiction are concerned. Roads are the responsibility of the provincial government. This program is an effort on the part of the resources department of the government to co-operate with the provinces. They do not have to accept if they do not want any program to better protect or manage their forests. There is no connection between these roads and roads to communities.
The second point is that this vote is concerned with forest access roads, and of course the roads to resources program is a different program entirely. It is another co-operative program with the provinces, but it is not 66968-9-73i
Supply-Northern Affairs under this vote. It is a new program in which Ontario has made a magnificent contribution by bringing this idea to the fore in Canada. Ontario is the pioneer in this field, and from a plan relating to mining access roads only it was later amended to cover access roads to all resources. All that the federal government has done has been to pick up this idea from Ontario and make it applicable all across Canada on a voluntary basis. The reason that we cannot divulge what is going on in the negotiations is that conditions change from time to time. If a road proposed by a province does not meet our criterion that the road should open new resources, we ask for a change and this may go back and forth. If these discussions were brought into public view then everybody would join in, and all logic and reason in the program would disappear. The province has the responsibility to serve the people with roads. These are roads to open up resources or to protect forests.

I should like to commend the
Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources for including this supplementary estimate of $1,682,000. I might say I am one of those who hold a great deal of admiration for the minister because I feel he is one of the hardest working and most sincere of our ministers. I only feel sorry for him when the big war tanks from the front lines of the opposition get rolling in this house.
I agree with the minister that the provinces should have the complete say in how this money should be spent. I do not think we should try to control the manner in which it is spent by the provinces. I might say that in my own province of Manitoba there was considerable agitation for a program of access roads. I am glad to see that it has come into being. It is a well-known fact that fire and pestilence destroy far more timber than is taken by the pulp and paper or lumbering industries. I am sure this program of access roads will do something to lower the fire hazards in the forests, and will also make it much more profitable for the pulp cutters, enabling them to bring out the wood from the more inaccessible areas. This will, in turn, lower their costs and it will save labour.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LIMIT ON AMOUNT TO BE BORROWED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution is to give assent to the introduction of a measure to amend section 13 of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act, 1951, for the purpose of increasing the statutory limit of the borrowing power of the authority from $300 million to $335 million. The proposed amendment does not in itself provide the authority with more funds. It has to do solely with the limiting of borrowing power. Capital expenditures of the seaway are financed by loans which the Minister of Finance is authorized to make under the powers contained in section 25 of the act but such loans may not be made in any fiscal year except to the extent that parliament has authorized them. Consequently capital expenditures on the seaway have been provided for from annual loan appropriations included in the estimates.
The need for increasing the borrowing limit became apparent last year when there was placed before parliament the approved capital budget for 1958, in compliance with section 80 of the Financial Administration Act. The statement then presented, in addition to showing the requirements for 1958, indicated that the aggregate capital expenditure was then estimated at $322,062,800.
St. Lawrence Seav>ay Authority Act It is expected that disbursements under parliamentary appropriations authorized to date will by March 31st next have amounted to about $270 million, leaving an unexhausted borrowing power of $30 million for future requirements.
The 1959 capital budget, which has not yet been tabled, will show an estimated expenditure in the year of $52,500,000, reduced for the time being to $30 million, so as not to exceed the present statutory borrowing limit. Vote No. 482 of the main estimates of 1959-60 contains a loan appropriation for the latter amount. A revised estimate has been made of total expenditure, which is now placed at $329,025,700. It is not possible, even at this date, to make a close estimate of final costs, because of such contingencies as contractors' claims, and the unsettled matter of any contribution which the governor in council may assess against the authority in connection with the Canadian National Railways' Victoria bridge diversion. It is therefore considered that in increasing the borrowing power from $300 million to $335 million the latter figure being about $6 million in excess of the official budget figure, reasonable provision would be made for undetermined requirements.

As questions have been placed on the order paper and references have been made in the press respecting claims filed by contractors in connection with St. Lawrence

seaway work, it is perhaps desirable that I should make a statement on this subject, based upon information furnished by the seaway authority.
In the first place, it might be said that it is not unusual or abnormal that claims are put forward in the case of large contracts, whether they be with public authorities or business corporations. To date the seaway authority has received claims in respect of 28 contracts, the individual amounts ranging from a few thousand to several million dollars. Except for minor items which on investigation may be paid for as units of work to which the contract is applicable, the claims relate to extra payments not authorized under the contracts and represent the contractors' own appraisal of costs, and sometimes profits, to which they claim to be entitled as a result of special situations and difficulties which were encountered in the course of the work. The totals are not necessarily a criterion of liability.
As background information it may be observed that the St. Lawrence seaway authority is not permitted under its bylaws to grant a construction contract exceeding $50,000 in value without the approval of treasury board being first obtained and no contract involving over $15,000 may be awarded without calling for sealed tenders on approved tender forms. The form of contract is that generally in use by government departments. No claim involving expenditure not provided for under the contract may be paid, in whole or in part, without the approval of treasury board.
Contractors for lock construction and channel excavation, whose claims represent about 86 per cent of the total received, have based them on general as well as specific representations. On general grounds they contend that favourable consideration should be given because a creditable job was done, essentially in time, but that in order to do so unanticipated and increased costs were involved and severe losses incurred. The authority points out that to complete in time was a primary obligation under the contracts and that each individual claim has to be considered on its merits and recommendations made in accordance with the principles laid down by treasury board. The authority is of the view that, in some cases, additional costs would have been avoided had the work been effectively and efficiently executed throughout the period. The records show that as regards several large contracts the work became admittedly so seriously behind schedule that the contractors involved were 66968-9-744
St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act obliged to change the management of their contracts. Complications naturally result from such occurrences.
While the claims cover numerous items of work, and as such are to be treated as individual in character, many of them fall into one or more of the following general categories: Claims due to a rising wage level; claims based upon alleged undisclosed ground and water conditions; claims based upon alleged interferences with scheduling of work for various causes, including changes in plans and delays in providing plans by engineers of the authority; claims due to quantities being greater than estimated in tender documents; claims due to quantities being less than estimated in tender documents; claims due to additional cost of placing concrete in winter; claims relating to quantities in dispute; claims based upon the contention that procedures for the disposal of excavating materials differed in actuality from that assumed at the time of tendering.
Pressure of urgent work, particularly in the final stages of construction, prevented the authority's engineers from giving priority to claims, although a good deal of time was given to discussions with contractors concerning them. About a year ago, two experienced engineers, Mr. W. B. Crombie, and Mr. D. Forgan, were employed for the special purpose of investigating and reporting on claims. Mr. Crombie was formerly a project manager and latterly consultant, at the head office of hydro-electric power commission of Ontario. Mr. Forgan previously held the position of director of construction, also with Ontario hydro. Considerable progress has been made and their findings are being reviewed by the chief engineer and his senior assistants who, as construction work nears completion, are in a position to devote more time to this activity. As soon as possible the authority will make a comprehensive report on each contractor's submission dealing not only with claims considered to be entitled to favourable consideration, but also with those considered inadmissible. The Minister of Transport will then refer the report to treasury board.
In general, claims will receive consideration and fair appraisal if extra or abnormal costs have been caused by action or omission on the part of the authority, or have arisen from physical conditions that could not have been foreseen. Or, on the other hand, extra costs attributable to errors or delays by the contractor or due to physical conditions which should have been foreseen or to increases in wages, there being no escalator clause, cannot be considered as the authority's responsibility.
Up to January 27, 28 claims have been received, totalling $36,329,000. Six of these

St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act claims have been dealt with and the remainder are being examined at the present time. It is expected that all major claims will have been dealt with within the next three months. The six claims that have been dealt with so far total $8,636,000. Of this amount, claims totalling $768,000 have been accepted and $7,868,000 have been rejected.
